title: “REJOICE IN THE WIFE OF YOUR YOUTH”: BIBLICAL FAITHFULNESS WAS NEVER MEANT TO BE COLD
paragraphs: “REJOICE IN THE WIFE OF YOUR YOUTH”: BIBLICAL FAITHFULNESS WAS NEVER MEANT TO BE COLD

Proverbs 5:18 does not merely tell a husband to stay. It calls him to rediscover joy in the woman he once chose—and exposes the quiet distance that can grow inside a marriage long before anyone walks away.
There is a kind of adultery that happens before a body ever enters another bed.
It begins with distance.
A conversation you stopped having.
A touch you stopped giving.
A tenderness you assumed would always be there.
Two people can still wear their wedding rings, still sleep beneath the same roof, still sit beside each other at church, still smile for family photographs…
and slowly become strangers.
No affair.
No divorce papers.
No public scandal.
Just a marriage quietly starving while everybody thinks it is still alive.
And into that uncomfortable silence, Scripture says something startling:
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
—Proverbs 5:18
The Hebrew is even more vivid.
יְהִי־מְקוֹרְךָ בָרוּךְ וּשְׂמַח מֵאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶךָ
Yehi-meqorkha varukh, usmach me'eshet ne'urekha.
“Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
That word translated “rejoice” comes from the Hebrew שָׂמַח — samach.
It carries the sense of rejoicing, being glad, taking joy.
God did not merely say:
Tolerate her.
Provide for her.
Stay legally married to her.
Avoid committing adultery.
He said:
Rejoice.
That changes everything.
Because biblical faithfulness was never supposed to mean cold coexistence.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to admit something painful:
You have remained physically present…
but your heart has been slowly checking out.
Maybe there was no catastrophic moment.
Maybe there was simply exhaustion.
Children came.
Bills came.
Responsibilities came.
Disappointments came.
Arguments accumulated.
Apologies became shorter.
Kisses became routine.
Date nights disappeared.
The person you once could not wait to see became the person you barely look at across the dinner table.
And somewhere between surviving Monday and paying Friday's bills, marriage became administration.
Schedules.
Groceries.
School.
Work.
Laundry.
Money.
Sleep.
Repeat.
Then Proverbs 5 walks directly into that ordinary exhaustion and reminds a husband:
She is not merely your roommate.
She is not merely the mother of your children.
She is not merely the woman helping you manage your household.
She is “the wife of your youth.”
There is memory in those words.
History.
Covenant.
A younger version of you once looked at this woman differently.
You noticed her laugh.
You remembered tiny details.
You wanted another five minutes beside her.
You looked forward to hearing her voice.
You found reasons to touch her hand.
You probably did things then that would embarrass you now.
And perhaps that is precisely the tragedy.
Not that you grew older.
But that somewhere along the way, familiarity convinced you to stop seeing the miracle standing beside you.
Proverbs 5 is not sentimental poetry floating above real life.
Its context is intensely serious.

The father is warning his son about sexual temptation and the destructive seduction of adultery. Rather than merely commanding him to run away from forbidden intimacy, Scripture redirects his desire toward covenant intimacy.
The next verse becomes remarkably intimate:
“Let her be as the loving hind and pleasant roe; let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
—Proverbs 5:19
Scripture is not embarrassed by marital desire.
God created marriage.
God created covenant affection.
God created the capacity for a husband and wife to delight in one another.
Sin did not invent intimacy.
God did.
And within the covenant of marriage, Scripture does not treat affection as dirty.
It protects it.
That matters in a world where sexual desire is constantly detached from covenant.
The culture says desire needs novelty.
Scripture points desire home.
The culture says excitement requires someone different.
Proverbs says, in effect:
Look again at the covenant you already made.
Remember.
Return.
Rejoice.
This does not mean pretending every marriage is healthy.
It does not mean ignoring abuse, coercion, betrayal, addiction, manipulation, or serious danger.

Biblical covenant faithfulness never requires calling evil good. Scripture repeatedly condemns oppression and wrongdoing, and someone facing abuse should seek safety, wise pastoral counsel, and appropriate professional or legal help.
Nor does Proverbs 5 mean that every struggling marriage can be repaired by arranging a romantic dinner and buying flowers.
Some wounds are deep.
Some trust has been shattered.
Some conversations require counseling.
Some marriages are carrying years of unresolved grief.
But there is still a question worth asking:
When did you stop pursuing the person you promised to love?
Not when did you stop paying the bills.
Not when did you stop coming home.
Not when did you stop wearing the ring.
When did you stop pursuing?
Because there is a difference between remaining married…
and nurturing a marriage.
There is a difference between occupying the same house…
and sharing a life.
There is a difference between faithfulness that merely says, “I didn't cheat”…
and covenant love that says,
“I am still choosing you.”
And before husbands turn this article into ammunition against their wives, remember where Proverbs places the responsibility.
The command confronts the man.
You rejoice.
It does not say:
“Rejoice if she never disappoints you.”
“Rejoice if she still looks twenty-five.”
“Rejoice if she always understands you.”
“Rejoice if she meets every emotional need perfectly.”
Marriage joins two sinners.
That means covenant love eventually discovers something infatuation never had to face:
the person you love is imperfect.
And so are you.
That is where marriage begins teaching us something much deeper than romance.
It begins teaching us about grace.
Not cheap grace that excuses sin.
Not fake peace that buries wounds.
Grace that looks truth in the face and still seeks redemption.
And suddenly marriage starts pointing beyond marriage.
Toward Christ.
Paul writes:
—Ephesians 5:25
Read that slowly.
Christ did not love His people because His people were flawless.
He loved sacrificially.
He gave Himself.
Christian marriage therefore cannot ultimately be sustained by butterflies.
Butterflies are wonderful.
But butterflies cannot carry a covenant through cancer.
They cannot carry it through unemployment.
They cannot carry it through sleepless nights with babies.
They cannot carry it through grief.
They cannot carry it through aging.
They cannot carry it through seasons when two exhausted people look at each other and realize they have almost forgotten how to talk.
Covenant needs something stronger.
It needs grace.
It needs forgiveness.
It needs repentance.
It needs Christ.
Maybe your marriage does not need another inspirational quote tonight.
Maybe it needs one person courageous enough to say:
“I've been distant.”
“I've taken you for granted.”
“I stopped listening.”
“I became defensive.”
“I have been physically here but emotionally somewhere else.”
“I've expected you to change while refusing to examine myself.”
“I am sorry.”
There are three words pride hates:
I was wrong.
And three words wounded marriages desperately need:
Please forgive me.
Repentance is not humiliation.
For the Christian, repentance is the doorway through which grace enters places pride has kept locked.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because some people reading this are carrying more than marital regret.
You are carrying secret sin.
Pornography.
Fantasy.
Emotional attachment to somebody who is not your spouse.
Messages you would panic if your husband or wife saw.
A relationship you keep calling “innocent” because admitting what it has become would require you to change.
Perhaps nobody knows.
But God does.
Proverbs 5:21 says:
“For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings.”
That sentence should sober us.
But it should not drive the repentant sinner away from Christ.
It should drive us to Him.
Because Christianity is not the story of respectable people successfully hiding their scandals.
It is the story of sinners being brought into the light…
and meeting a Savior there.
Jesus does not call sin harmless.
He died because sin is deadly.
But the cross also declares something astonishing:
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
—Romans 8:1
That does not mean there are no consequences.
It means condemnation does not have the final word over the one who belongs to Christ.
So if you have crossed boundaries…
repent.
If you are approaching boundaries…
run.
If something needs to be confessed…
bring it into the light with wisdom and appropriate support.
If you have stopped pursuing your spouse…
begin again.
If your marriage is wounded…
seek help.
If you have become cold…
ask God to soften what disappointment hardened.
And if you have failed spectacularly, do not confuse shame with repentance.
Shame whispers:
Hide.
Jesus calls:
Come.
Shame says:
You are permanently defined by what you did.
The Gospel says that in Christ there is forgiveness, cleansing, a new identity, and a new way to walk.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9
That is why our message will always return here:
Not because scandal does not matter.
Not because betrayal is painless.
Not because consequences disappear.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
He takes sinners who thought hiding would save them and teaches them to walk in light.
He takes proud hearts and teaches them repentance.
He takes wounded people and teaches them forgiveness without pretending the wound never happened.
He takes lust and calls us toward holiness.
He takes selfishness and teaches sacrificial love.
He takes dead places and, according to His wisdom and will, can breathe life where people thought nothing beautiful could grow again.
Maybe tonight your first act of obedience is surprisingly small.
Put the phone down.
Look at your wife.
Look at your husband.
Really look.
Remember the person behind the responsibilities.
Remember the story.
Remember what you have survived.
Remember the prayers God answered.
Remember the laughter.
Remember the tears.
Remember that covenant should never become an excuse to stop cherishing the person you promised to love.
And husbands…
hear Proverbs again.
וּשְׂמַח מֵאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶךָ
Usmach me'eshet ne'urekha.
Rejoice in the wife of your youth.
Not merely endure.
Not merely coexist.
Not merely avoid divorce.
Rejoice.
Perhaps you cannot manufacture feelings on command.
But you can begin cultivating what neglect has been starving.
You can listen.
You can confess.
You can pray.
You can put boundaries around temptation.
You can become curious about your spouse again.
You can speak tenderness instead of assuming they already know.
You can seek biblical counseling when the wounds are beyond what the two of you know how to repair alone.
You can ask Christ to teach you how to love when your natural resources feel exhausted.
And wives reading this, the Gospel does not reduce you to an object responsible for keeping your husband's attention.
You bear God's image.

Marriage calls both husband and wife into covenant faithfulness, honor, love, and mutual marital responsibility. First Corinthians 7 speaks with striking reciprocity about husband and wife belonging faithfully to one another, while Hebrews 13:4 calls marriage honorable and the marriage bed undefiled.
The Christian vision is not one spouse consuming the other.
It is covenant.
Faithfulness.
Holiness.
Sacrifice.
Joy.
And ultimately…
Christ.
Maybe this article exposed something you have been avoiding.
Pray.
Then, where appropriate, talk to your spouse.
And if your heart is saying, God, I have allowed something precious to become cold, be honest before Him.
Someone quietly losing hope may need to hear that restoration can require time, truth, repentance, boundaries, forgiveness, counseling, and above all the grace of God.
Not because you need another post sitting forgotten in a folder…
but because there may come a night when resentment is louder than remembrance.
Come back and read Proverbs 5 again.
Send it privately to somebody fighting for a marriage nobody else knows is hurting.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, you can help us continue producing and expanding Christ-centered resources.

Scripture teaches voluntary generosity, not spiritual coercion: “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Your responsibility to honor God with your resources extends far beyond any online ministry, including faithful generosity through your local church and care for people in need.
Think of it as more than paying for content.
Think of what your support can help make possible:
another exhausted believer encountering Scripture at 2:00 in the morning…
another marriage being confronted before temptation becomes catastrophe…
another prodigal remembering Jesus…
another wounded Christian opening the Bible again…
another person discovering that grace is not permission to remain in sin but the power of Christ calling sinners out of darkness.
Do it prayerfully.
Do it because you believe Gospel-centered discipleship is worth helping continue.
A share costs nothing, yet it may place biblical truth in front of the exact person who was never going to search for it themselves.
Because eventually every marriage discovers this:
You did not marry someone who would never need grace.
You married someone who would.
And they married someone who would need it too.
You.
So go home to the covenant.
Go back to the conversation.
Go back to prayer.
Go back to truth.
Go back to tenderness.
Go back to repentance where repentance is needed.
Go back to forgiveness where forgiveness can rightly begin.
And above everything else…
go back to Jesus.
Because perhaps the most dangerous moment in a marriage is not when two people finally admit something is broken.
Perhaps it is when they stop believing anything is worth fighting to restore.
The ring may tell the world whom you married—but the way you love when nobody is watching reveals whether covenant is still alive in your heart.
